newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: SOCCER-LISBON CLUBS SPEND TO END PORTO DOMINANCE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-LISBON CLUBS SPEND TO END PORTO DOMINANCE.

text.p: Top Lisbon clubs Benfica and Sporting have been on record spending sprees in the off season in a bid to stop Porto lifting a fourth consecutive Portuguese league title.
Benfica and Sporting have splashed out some $14 million dollars each on players they hope will make them good enough to break Porto's three-year grip on the championship.

Brazilian international Paulo Nunes became the country's most expensive import when Benfica invested $5 million in just a half share in the talented former Gremio striker. The other half remains with the player's business manager.
Sporting spent a total $10 million on two more Brazilians -- Leandro Machado from Spain's Valencia and Carlos Miguel, Nunes' former club colleague.

With last season's top scorer Mario Jardel leading the Porto attack and a clutch of lesser Brazilians spread around other sides, soccer chiefs hope for an infusion of some Latin American magic into a league championship which has lacked sparkle in recent seasons.
In part this has been due to the clear superiority of Porto, who had both the last two championships wrapped up long before the end of the season.
Crowds have dwindled as some leading Portuguese players such as Luis Figo and Vitor Baia of Barcelona left in search of the bigger wages and more glamorous clubs.
Former European champions Benfica, who last won the domestic championship in 1993-94, have virtually rebuilt their side after suffering one of their worst campaigns ever last season.
They finished a distant third in the league, 27 points behind Porto, and then lost the Portuguese Cup final to Porto's Oporto neighbours Boavista.

So determined are Benfica that they even turned down a tempting $14 million offer from Spain for key striker and captain Joao Vieira Pinto, although in truth, sale of the charismatic Joao Pinto, a favourite of the fiercely partisan Benfica fans, would have probably sparked a riot.

Sporting, who finished second to Porto last season, have spent just as much as their Lisbon rivals but their investment has been concentrated in fewer players as they seek their first championship in 15 seasons.
"Given what we achieved last year, it would be logical to set our sights that little bit higher this year," said coach Octavio Machado.

With a relatively easy pre-qualifying draw -- they face either Israel's Beitar or Sileks of Macedonia -- Sporting also look well set to take part in the European Cup Champions League for the first time since 1982.
This season sees the competition extended to include runners-up from the major European leagues.
But the heavy spending has also raised some eyebrows at a time when many leading clubs are in trouble with the tax authorities over unpaid tax and social security bills.
Porto's tough-talking boss Jorge Nuno Pinto da Costa, whose club says it has no outstanding debts, took the opportunity for some verbal point-scoring.
"If Porto did not pay its taxes, it would also have money to buy lots of players," he said recently.

Porto have been among the least active on the transfer market, clearly confident that Jardel, who scored more goals than anyone bar world footballer of the year Ronaldo last season, will again be in fine striking form.
The only additions to the Porto squad will be Bulgarian Emil Kostadinov, who returns from Turkey's Fenerbahce, and a couple of Portuguese signings.
"You don't meddle with a winning side," said Pinto da Costa confidently.
